To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) investors systematically overreact to changes in the target rate; and (b) the overreaction is small enough to be consistent with the observed dependence of excess returns to the slope of the Treasury yield curve.

(1) the slope of the Treasury yield curve is a good proxy for the path of the Federal funds rate; (2) a small degree of investor overreaction to changes in the path is enough to explain the dependence of excess returns to Treasuries on yield curve slope; and (3) the model can account for the well-documented dependence of the slope of the term structure of interest rates on the path of the federal funds rate, as well as for the dependence of excess bond returns
the market price of risk depends on the slope of yield curve and that this effect is due to a small degree of systematic investor overreaction.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the slope of the term structure is a useful predictor of future excess returns in Treasury bills, but only if the slope is used in a manner that takes into account the fact that the slope is not a stationary variable.
the yield curve slope is a useful indicator of future changes in the level of the short-term interest rates, but it is not a reliable predictor of the sign of the change in the interest rate.
the market price of risk in Treasuries is not constant over the yield curve, as is usually assumed, but depends on the slope of this yield curve.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a small degree overreaction by investors in the presence of a target rate can account for a significant portion of the observed dependence of excess returns of Treasuries on changes in the slope of the curve.

we have developed a model of the term structure of interest rates that can account for a number of salient features of the empirical data, including the dependence of the market price of risk on the slope of yield curve.
a small degree (less than 10%) of overreaction in the market price of risk can explain the empirical regularity of the dependence of excess returns to Treasuries on slope of the yield curves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the market price of risk can be a function of the slope of the term structure of interest rates.
the dependence of excess returns of Treasury securities on the slope of their own yield curve may be explained without the need to appeal to any form of time-varying risk premia.

the market price of risk depends on the slope of yield curve because of a combination of two factors: a) the slope is an important signal of the future direction of the target rate, and b) investors overreact to this signal.
